item.title: China's Ministry of Commerce and Science Ministry propose new AI export controls including 23 AI technologies with interim pre-export registration effective immediately [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 in October 2026, proposing to add 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, including 23 related to artificial intelligence. The announcement introduces an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect, covering frontier AI model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capabilities with specific technical thresholds. The draft catalogue is open for public comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies immediately to exports, including those already in progress. The controls distinguish between service access and physical export, with API and lightweight use exempted but local deployment outside China considered an export. The measures also cover licensing, ownership transfers, and intra-group code sharing, potentially affecting multinational companies. The announcement aims to prevent uncontrolled technology diffusion while allowing legitimate cooperation and is part of China's broader technology export control framework.

item.title: Proton publishes AI manifesto outlining software engineering transformation and cultural shift amid AI-driven code automation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Proton has released an internal AI manifesto addressing the profound changes AI models have brought to software engineering, emphasizing the need for a cultural shift where engineers guide AI tools rather than write code manually. The manifesto highlights that traditional coding is becoming obsolete as AI can handle routine tasks, and stresses the importance of adapting quickly to remain competitive and secure in the evolving tech landscape. The document outlines three key areas Proton must address to succeed in this transition, including changing engineer mindsets to manage AI agents effectively and improving AI autonomy. It also acknowledges the broader industry impact of AI on software development productivity and warns that failure to adapt could threaten organizational missions. Proton positions this shift as an opportunity for engineers to leverage their expertise in collaboration with AI rather than being replaced by it.

item.title: Nolan Lawson benchmarks AI-generated JavaScript frameworks using a Pokémon app to evaluate development cost, code quality, and performance across multiple frameworks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nolan Lawson conducted a benchmark study to assess the AI cost of various JavaScript frameworks by instructing agents to build a small Pokémon app using different frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and SvelteKit. The study measured development time, token usage, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores using Lighthouse, aiming to provide evidence-based insights into framework efficiency rather than relying on subjective developer preferences. The experiment involved running multiple iterations per framework to account for variability in AI output and Lighthouse metrics, with a focus on a content-based app that is simple yet non-trivial. Lawson avoided specifying architecture details or CSS frameworks to keep the comparison focused on JavaScript frameworks and their meta-frameworks. The results highlight the stochastic nature of AI-generated code and the challenges in benchmarking, but offer a data-driven perspective on the trade-offs involved in choosing frameworks for AI-assisted development.

item.title: Researchers prove the Platonic Representation Hypothesis using Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), showing models trained on different modalities learn aligned representations up to rotation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have proven the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), demonstrating that Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained on multiple modalities converge to the same representation of the world up to a rotation when trained on positive pairs representing the same scene. They show that next-token prediction is a form of JEPA with less aligned views, explaining why language models align with vision models only at large scale. The study validates these findings on datasets ranging from 145,000 captions to 940 million web images and reveals a scaling law predicting alignment efficiency, with positive views requiring significantly fewer training samples than next-token prediction to achieve similar alignment.

item.title: Researchers introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression for long-horizon LLM agents, reducing computation by over 50% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free method that uses soft tokens within large language model (LLM) agents to compress context in long-horizon tasks. ASTC leverages the model's native recurrent dynamics and hybrid Gated Delta Network attention to carry forward absorbed information as soft tokens, reducing later-layer computation and enabling reusable key-value caches. Experiments show ASTC matches or exceeds the accuracy of uncompressed agents while using up to 50.68% fewer attention pairs, outperforming trained compressors that require significantly more attention pairs per successful task. This approach offers a model-native way to efficiently manage growing interaction contexts in sustained LLM tasks.

item.title: Researchers introduce GAIM and Q-DAIM kernel-based methods for compressing attention mechanism contexts, enabling linear-time compression and streaming updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose two novel KV-cache compression methods, GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on kernel interpolation techniques to address the quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms in language models. These methods leverage the Hilbert space formulation of attention and introduce surrogate models for linear-time compression, extending to streaming attention scenarios with adaptive interpolation updates. Numerical experiments demonstrate convergence and competitive performance on the LongBench-E benchmark, suggesting that Q-DAIM can efficiently identify key information in the KV cache for compression.

item.title: Researchers introduce EDB-Bio benchmark to evaluate language models' ability to assess scientific evidence in biology, showing improved calibration and efficiency after training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed EDB-Bio, a scientific reasoning benchmark with 96,000 episodes from drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human genome-wide association studies, to test language models' capacity to evaluate empirical evidence and predict hypothesis validity. Initial models showed underconfidence and poor calibration, but training with proper scoring rules enhanced their performance and efficiency in sequential experiment selection tasks. The study quantifies how models update beliefs using Bayes factors and compares their judgments to expert biologists, revealing areas of agreement and bias. The work advances calibration and uncertainty analysis in scientific forecasting, with applications in cancer biology, and all related code, data, and models have been released.

item.title: Researchers propose Muon-RT to eliminate momentum buffers in large language model self-distillation, improving accuracy and reducing memory use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), a method that reuses teacher-student displacement to remove momentum buffers in large language model self-distillation, reducing persistent memory requirements. Muon-RT encodes an exponentially weighted history of updates, smooths noise, and applies spectral normalization and orthogonalization to improve training efficiency. Experiments with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show Muon-RT improves average accuracy by 2.6 points over AdamW with 42% less memory and by 5.4 points over momentum Muon with 27% less memory. Self-Distillation Policy Optimization on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct also yields a 2.0-point accuracy improvement over AdamW.

item.title: SparseGDN introduces chunk-sparse linear attention with hardware-aware approximations and dynamic recurrent-event selection, achieving up to 1.94x prefill speedups on Qwen3.5 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SparseGDN is a new framework that improves the efficiency of Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) for linear-time sequence modeling by combining structured intra-chunk approximations with input-dependent recurrent-event selection. It reduces computation and memory usage by selectively updating recurrent states and reconstructing token outputs from compact state snapshots, enabling outputs for every token while lowering overhead. The approach uses a block-adjacent solver to minimize local Delta-solve computations and dynamically allocates recurrent-update budgets across attention head pairs. Evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B models across RULER tasks with context lengths from 4K to 128K tokens show that SparseGDN retains about 29% of recurrent events on average and achieves 1.50 to 1.94 times speedups over native FLA kernels, including the cost of online selection.

item.title: Researchers present TSBPO, a tree-structured policy optimization method for interactive language agents achieving over 96% success on ALFWorld and 81% on WebShop benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce TSBPO, a training paradigm that addresses sampling, delayed feedback assignment, and token loss aggregation in interactive language agents within a single training loop. Using a likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator, TSBPO targets task continuations likely to yield contrasting outcomes under fixed rollout budgets, and applies trajectory and step advantages to compare segments and outcomes in replayed physical trees. Evaluated with a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, TSBPO achieved 97.79% success on seen tasks and 96.64% on unseen tasks in ALFWorld, and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for 500 WebShop test goals.

item.title: Researchers introduce EvoMemBench, a benchmark evaluating memory mechanisms in LLM agents across memory scope and content, comparing 15 methods under a standardized protocol [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present EvoMemBench, a unified benchmark designed to systematically assess memory mechanisms in large language model (LLM) agents from a self-evolving perspective. The benchmark evaluates memory along two axes-memory scope (in-episode vs. cross-episode) and memory content (knowledge-oriented vs. execution-oriented)-and compares 15 representative memory methods against strong long-context baselines. The study finds that current memory systems are not yet general solutions: long-context baselines remain competitive, memory aids most when context is insufficient or tasks are complex, and no single memory type performs consistently across all scenarios. Retrieval-based methods excel in knowledge-intensive tasks, while procedural and long-term memory methods are more effective for execution-oriented tasks when aligned with task structure. The dataset and code are publicly available to support further research on improving memory systems for LLM-based agents.

item.title: Researchers introduce DialFork benchmark to evaluate procedural hallucination in conversational agents across 24 tasks and 12 domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed DialFork, the first benchmark designed to measure procedural hallucination in large language model-based conversational agents, where agents produce plausible but procedurally incorrect dialogue. DialFork contains 36,278 dialogues created by forking conformant dialogues at controlled points and injecting four types of hallucinations, validated by 30 human annotators. The benchmark defines three evaluation tasks to assess procedural deviation at different granularities and proposes new dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, which outperform existing baselines in detecting procedural errors. DialFork is released under open licenses to encourage the community to evaluate conversational process fidelity alongside content accuracy.

item.title: Researchers present AnytimeReasoner framework with Budget Relative Policy Optimization to improve token efficiency and reasoning flexibility in large language models under varying token budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce AnytimeReasoner, a framework designed to optimize anytime reasoning performance in large language models by improving token efficiency and enabling flexible reasoning under different token budget constraints. The approach involves truncating reasoning processes to fit sampled token budgets and summarizing optimal answers for verification, which provides dense rewards for reinforcement learning optimization. They also propose Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), a variance reduction technique to enhance learning robustness and efficiency. Empirical tests on mathematical reasoning tasks show that AnytimeReasoner consistently outperforms existing methods like GRPO across various token budgets and prior distributions, improving both training and token efficiency. This work addresses limitations of prior reinforcement learning approaches that optimize only final performance under fixed large token budgets, offering a more adaptable and efficient solution for scaling reasoning capabilities in large language models.

item.title: Researchers introduce Mstar, a method that evolves task-specific memory programs for large language model agents, improving performance across conversation, embodied planning, and expert reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present Mstar, a method that automatically discovers optimized memory harnesses for large language model agents by evolving executable Python memory programs tailored to specific tasks. Mstar jointly optimizes components defining memory schema, logic, and instructions to better handle diverse requirements such as conversation, embodied planning, and specialized reasoning. Evaluations on four distinct tasks show that Mstar outperforms existing baselines and produces structurally distinct memory programs suited to each domain. These results suggest that customizing memory harnesses per task enhances agent performance and that memory-program search is an effective approach to achieve this.

item.title: Researchers formalize controllable user simulation as a causal inference problem to improve evaluation of conversational agents and propose methods to eliminate bias and preserve behavioral diversity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers address limitations in evaluating conversational agents using offline datasets by formalizing controllable user simulation as a causal inference problem. They identify that standard training methods introduce look-ahead bias linked to the behavior policy, causing evaluation metric variance to explode under policy shifts, a phenomenon termed controllability collapse. To fix this, they propose theoretical conditions and practical training methods including a priori controls, step-wise dynamic controls, and policy-conditioned learning. Empirical results show their approach removes bias, maintains natural variance, and generalizes well to unseen agent behaviors, unlike standard global controls that distort distributions and reduce diversity.

item.title: SIRF model internalizes complex platform policies for industrial content risk control, achieving 71.3% Black Recall@P95 with low latency and improved mis-penalization recovery [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model) is designed for industrial content risk control, focusing on high precision and second-level latency rather than average accuracy. It internalizes complex platform policies into model weights through continued pretraining without additional human annotation, enabling ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment that applies rules precisely. A controlled comparison with a baseline model shows SIRF-8B-SFT improves Black Recall@P95 by 15.1 percentage points using about 70 million continued pretraining tokens, without reducing general ability. Deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer, SIRF recovers 20% more mis-penalized samples and reduces mis-penalization by approximately 70% in freezing scenarios, demonstrating effective policy internalization and transfer at low cost.

item.title: Researchers introduce a unified four-coefficient per-token gating parameterization for on-policy knowledge distillation, combining forward and reverse KL losses with multi-channel and bias terms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a new four-coefficient parameterization for per-token gating in on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), unifying existing methods like EOPD and ToDi by allowing multi-channel composition and explicit bias. Experiments on TweetEval tasks using a Qwen3-32B teacher and Qwen3-4B student show that configurations within this family outperform single-channel gating approaches in most cases. The study presents this parameterization as a shared framework for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD, supported by exploratory aggregate evidence and targeted replications that are directionally consistent but not statistically significant at small sample sizes.

item.title: Researchers report three preregistered studies analyzing harness effects on a longevity-tuned 1.7B language model, finding mixed gains mostly linked to unparsed data and constant label baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted three preregistered studies to evaluate the impact of harnesses on a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7 billion parameter language model. They found that reported performance gains often stemmed from unparsed input rows and that replication attempts missed these effects. Across various tests, harnesses sometimes improved accuracy over capped settings but were often comparable to constant answer baselines or simpler methods. The studies included evaluations on different model sizes and tasks, such as mortality prediction and question answering benchmarks. Some harnesses outperformed others in specific settings, but overall gains were inconsistent and frequently aligned with label distribution biases rather than meaningful improvements. The findings suggest that harness benefits depend on task characteristics and label skew, with no clear advantage demonstrated across all question types or models.

item.title: Tim Berners-Lee's vision of autonomous software agents for the web is realized with AI-powered agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots transforming online interactions [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: In 2001, Tim Berners-Lee and colleagues proposed the Semantic Web, envisioning autonomous software agents navigating the internet to fulfill user needs without manual browsing. While the original idea required extensive tagging of web content and did not gain traction, recent advances in large language models have enabled AI agents to understand and interact with web content autonomously, fulfilling Berners-Lee's vision in new ways. Today, AI agents such as Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, and Anthropic's Claude Duet are widely used to perform tasks like booking appointments and searching for information, changing how users engage with the web. This emerging "agentic web" is reshaping online experiences, with companies adapting content and services for agent interaction, though its long-term impact on web openness and control remains uncertain.

item.title: Ryanair considers pay freezes, reducing flight crew, and increasing AI use to offset €2bn fuel cost rise amid Middle East conflict [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Ryanair is evaluating cost-cutting measures including pay freezes, reducing the number of crew members on flights, and expanding the use of artificial intelligence to manage soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict. The airline expects its jet fuel expenses to increase by about €2 billion in the financial year ending March 2028, with European short-haul fares likely to rise by up to 20% as a result. The company said 80% of its fuel needs until March are hedged at $67 per barrel, but only 25% of the following year's requirements are hedged at $95 per barrel. Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary noted that while fare increases and competitor capacity reductions may offset some costs, they will not fully cover the fuel bill rise. The airline reported a 6% year-on-year profit decline to €1.61 billion in the quarter ending September, with passenger numbers growing 5% to 64.5 million.

item.title: Roblox reports over 70,000 AI-generated games published in five months as Steam acknowledges challenges with AI content quality [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Roblox has embraced AI-powered game development, launching its Build tool in July 2026 and enabling users to publish more than 70,000 games within five months. The company highlights rapid content creation and increased use of AI tools among top creators, positioning itself to capture a significant share of the global gaming market. In contrast, Valve has acknowledged issues with low-quality AI-generated games flooding its Steam platform but has yet to find a solution. Roblox emphasizes its social distribution model as a way to help quality content reach audiences despite the surge in AI-generated games, while also introducing initiatives to make games playable across devices and platforms.

item.title: Haas says PostgreSQL 19 release delayed due to focus on AI-driven bug discovery and quality concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Haas has stated that the release of PostgreSQL 19 has been delayed, attributing the delay to the project's emphasis on quality and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence technologies in identifying long-standing bugs. The delay is considered short-term and not particularly concerning in the broader context of the project's goals. He highlighted that AI, particularly large language models, can uncover bugs that humans missed over the past forty years, raising questions about how PostgreSQL will continue to innovate and catch up with these findings. Haas and others are actively working to address these challenges and determine the project's future direction.

item.title: Sam Altman says running AI models locally wastes limited DRAM resources amid ongoing memory shortages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman criticized the trend of running AI models locally on personal devices, arguing it inefficiently uses scarce DRAM memory that could be better utilized in cloud data centers. He highlighted that local AI setups often use only a small fraction of their memory capacity, exacerbating a global memory shortage expected to continue through 2030. Altman contrasted his view with partners like Nvidia and Microsoft, who promote local AI for privacy and reduced cloud dependence. He also noted that memory manufacturers are cautious about expanding production due to past overcapacity risks, contributing to the current supply constraints. The shortage has made AI-optimized PCs expensive, limiting mainstream adoption until prices decrease.

item.title: Researchers propose Li2SAO, a lightweight asynchronous RL optimization method with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping, improving early training and performance over GRPO and LiSAO on agentic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used for post-training large language models to improve efficiency by updating models as rollouts arrive. Recent methods like Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) improve stability but rely on closed-source pretrained value models. This paper introduces LiSAO, a lightweight SAO variant without pretrained value models, and finds it underperforms GRPO on reasoning tasks but excels on agentic tasks, though it lags in early training due to an untrained value model. To address early training limitations, the authors propose Li2SAO, which uses group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: training the actor with group-relative advantage and the critic with group-centered returns before switching to single-rollout generalized advantage estimation. Experiments show Li2SAO matches or surpasses GRPO early in training and achieves higher final performance. The code is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B-parameter hybrid computer-use agent trained via a five-stage curriculum using evolved teacher harnesses and skill-conditioned workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Mage-VL-Cowork integrates visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution in a single policy, trained from a multimodal checkpoint through midtraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. The training uses Mage-CUA-Forge to generate over 293,000 desktop and web tasks across nearly 7,000 skills, reducing per-task costs by 82.6% through reusable workflows and application-specific preparers. Instead of distilling a fixed teacher model, the team evolved teacher harnesses and specialized agent harnesses to produce high-quality training trajectories with stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B achieved 66.0% accuracy on the OSWorld-Verified benchmark with efficient reasoning costs, setting a new state-of-the-art for its parameter size and advancing on-device AI capabilities.

item.title: Researchers compare continuous diffusion language models and speculative drafters for unconditional text generation, finding LangFlow outperforms DSpark variants on longer sequences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers compared continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters by training LangFlow and DSpark architectures from scratch on unconditional OpenWebText generation at sequence lengths of 16, 128, and 1024 tokens without verification. They evaluated generation perplexity and distributional similarity, finding LangFlow outperforms DSpark variants at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at length 16. The study highlights iterative full-sequence refinement as a key factor in LangFlow's advantage on longer sequences, despite improvements from recurrent memory in DSpark models.

item.title: Researchers find pruning redundant attention heads in GPT-2-XL reduces verbatim memorisation by 91.5% while improving language modeling performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study shows that zeroing out a large number of redundant attention heads in the GPT-2-XL language model significantly suppresses its tendency to reproduce memorised sequences from training data, reducing memorisation by 91.5%. This pruning also improves the model's performance on the WikiText-103 benchmark, lowering perplexity by 0.92, suggesting that many attention heads are unnecessary for downstream tasks. The findings indicate that attention-head redundancy can be exploited at inference time to mitigate privacy and intellectual property risks without retraining or altering the training data.

item.title: Researchers introduce BlindToChange benchmark showing AI agents often fail to proactively detect recent real-world changes affecting their responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed BlindToChange, a benchmark designed to evaluate whether AI agents proactively discover recent events that impact their outputs without explicit user prompts. The study finds that while AI agents can find recent changes when directly asked, their performance drops significantly-by up to 27.5 points-when such changes are not explicitly mentioned in user requests. This gap highlights that many agents do not verify if relevant facts have changed, leading to incorrect or outdated responses. BlindToChange uses real-world events drawn from Wikidata and focuses on recommendation tasks where obvious options are invalidated by recent developments. The benchmark aims to track progress in AI systems' ability to account for recent, implicitly relevant information in their responses.

item.title: Researchers trace fine-tuned language model behaviors to KV cache patches, showing transfer and removal of behaviors via attention mechanism [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate where fine-tuned behaviors in language models arise by patching the key-value (KV) cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the base model and vice versa. They find that some behaviors, such as responding in German or emergent misalignment, can be transferred or removed through KV cache patching, indicating that altered processing of previous tokens via attention contributes to fine-tuned responses. The study reveals that the impact of patching increases with the amount of KV cache replaced and is concentrated at pivotal token positions, particularly system-prompt and chat-template tokens, which have disproportionate influence on model behavior.

item.title: Researchers present KEEPER, a method analyzing control-sufficient textual memory for long-horizon LLM agents, highlighting error persistence and reward-related prediction's impact on task performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce KEEPER, a framework evaluating four auxiliary objectives for recursive textual memory in long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents, focusing on how supervision targets affect agent performance. They identify self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims in memory and find that reward-related prediction objectives yield the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. The study includes a claim-level analysis showing that errors can persist despite corrective observations, emphasizing the need to assess error persistence and valid information retention alongside task outcomes. This work suggests that task performance alone does not guarantee reliable memory updates in LLM agents and proposes metrics to better evaluate memory reliability.

item.title: Researchers propose DualBudget sparse-expert diffusion model balancing attention graph edges and expert activation for long-context text tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce DualBudget, a sparse-expert diffusion configuration that manages two separate computational budgets-attention graph edges and expert activations per token-to improve long-context text processing. The model connects various attention mechanisms with conditional expert computation and is evaluated on tasks including scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. The study shows performance gains over baselines up to 16,000 tokens with some degradation at longer lengths and reports a 20% cost reduction compared to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. Ablation studies reveal mixed effects on evaluation metrics, and the analysis distinguishes measured results from unverified claims about training speed, global coherence, and deployment memory.

item.title: Researchers present BYOD, a parameter-efficient LoRA-based method to convert autoregressive language models to diffusion models across multiple architectures including Mistral [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a LoRA-only approach enabling efficient conversion of autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion language models (DLMs) without architecture-specific tuning. BYOD was applied to Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Mistral 8B models, with adapters comprising 4.1-5.8% of parameters and requiring up to 102.4 million tokens processed in under 4 hours on a single GPU. The converted models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context, and retain substantial knowledge from their parent AR models. BYOD-Gemma achieved 50.6% average accuracy on a nine-task evaluation, close to the 51.9% of LLaDA 8B Instruct, though open-generation quality at low network function evaluation budgets remains a limitation, with higher perplexity than AR parents. The team provides standalone training, evaluation implementations, and interactive demos for all four conversions, offering a practical path to extend diffusion generation to existing model families while highlighting areas for improving conversion efficiency.

item.title: Researchers identify unintended discourse changes caused by activation steering in large language models and propose a vector-based intervention to restore discourse while preserving intended behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Activation steering is a technique that modifies large language model outputs by adding vectors to their activations during inference, aiming to control behavior or tone without retraining. Researchers found that this method also causes significant unintended changes in discourse aspects such as formality, evidence use, and ambiguity, which prior work only measured through coarse metrics like perplexity. They developed a complementary vector intervention that counteracts these unintended discourse shifts, restoring about 78% of the changes while maintaining the intended steering effects in approximately 93% of cases.

item.title: Researchers introduce PEEL to extract taxonomic hierarchies from Matryoshka Representation Learning embeddings, recovering ontological structures without task-specific training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies), a minimal probe that decodes hierarchical taxonomic structures from frozen Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings by leveraging an order-embedding objective and minimum spanning arborescence. This method recovers taxonomic directed acyclic graphs with high fidelity on two benchmarks and transfers to new domains without target-edge supervision, using only concept vocabularies and no documents. The study finds that prefix lengths in MRL embeddings correspond to coarse-to-fine granularity in taxonomies, a pattern consistent across three distinct MRL models. PEEL offers a cost-effective alternative to clustering and large language model-based taxonomy construction methods, which require extensive tuning or expensive training.

item.title: SimXAI introduces a lightweight LLM-based conversational layer that improves interaction quality and understanding in conversational explainable AI by replacing traditional modular pipelines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SimXAI is a new conversational layer designed for explainable AI (XAI) agents that replaces separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and response generation with a single large language model (LLM) that accesses existing XAI resources. This approach aims to improve handling of context-dependent follow-up questions while maintaining faithfulness to underlying XAI methods. The researchers developed an evaluation suite to test parsing accuracy, faithfulness, and contextualization across multiple datasets, where SimXAI demonstrated strong function-selection accuracy and better contextual understanding. In a user study replacing the conversational layer of a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and with fewer conversational turns, indicating improved conversational quality and usability without sacrificing faithfulness.

item.title: Researchers propose TIZSKT for zero-shot cross-domain knowledge tracing using text as an index to predict student responses without target-domain training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce TIZSKT, a method for zero-shot cross-domain knowledge tracing that predicts a student's next response using question texts and behavioral history without requiring target-domain training data. The approach separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-specific evidence construction, employing a frozen text encoder and unsupervised projections to create fixed question addresses that aggregate historical correctness summaries. TIZSKT incorporates components such as the Mastery-Dynamics Encoder, Text-Addressing Kernel, Cross-Segment Continuation, and Evidence-Volume Read-Out to effectively model student performance across domains. Evaluations on three public datasets using leave-one-domain-out experiments show that TIZSKT outperforms existing baselines in mean AUC and accuracy, with ablation studies confirming the importance of text addressing and cross-segment continuation features.

item.title: Researchers propose framework aligning multimodal large language models with human cognitive structure using behavior-derived semantic dimensions from 4.7 million similarity judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a framework to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgments. They used a semantic embedding space based on 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.7 million human Odd-One-Out judgments, enabling MLLMs to learn both choices and justifications consistent with human decision criteria. Experimental results show improved model consistency with human similarity judgments while maintaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Using representational similarity analysis on an independent fMRI dataset, the study observed increased alignment between model and human brain representations. This work suggests a data-driven approach to incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLM alignment.

item.title: Researchers propose CRoS, a causality reward metric that scrambles reasoning steps without altering content to improve language model accuracy and reasoning faithfulness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a new metric for evaluating chain-of-thought (CoT) causality in language models by perturbing the order of reasoning steps without changing their content. This approach aims to better reinforce high-quality reasoning compared to existing methods that alter step content and may confound causality assessment. Evaluated on Reasoning Gym with the Gemma-3-4B model, CRoS outperforms prior causality and outcome reward metrics, achieving 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets versus 43.8% for the strongest baseline, and shows improvements in CoT quality and faithfulness. CRoS also attains a higher hint acknowledgment score, indicating better alignment between reasoning steps and final answers.

item.title: Researchers propose Zyphra Hierarchical Attention, a subquadratic sparse attention method using a hierarchical tree-structured indexer to improve long-context capabilities of large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA), a sparse attention method that uses a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer to reduce the quadratic scaling bottleneck in large language models' attention mechanisms. ZHA builds a tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to retrieve a sparse subset of keys, achieving subquadratic scaling in sequence length while maintaining performance on long-context retrieval and complex reasoning tasks. ZHA can be applied to existing pretrained models with minimal additional training and is robust to various tree geometries, including deep trees with up to six levels. The researchers provide a performance model showing that ZHA outperforms competing methods beyond one million context tokens and has the potential to extend effective context windows to hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

item.title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview launches an open speech-language model integrating speech processing, reasoning, and tool use with text and image inputs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Apriel Voice 27B Preview is an open speech-language model designed to unify speech recognition, contextual reasoning, conversation, and tool interaction within a shared reasoning framework. Built on the Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, it processes speech directly and generates responses and tool calls without a separate dialogue model, supporting interactive voice interactions on a custom serving platform. The model uses a two-stage training process to adapt to speech, involving establishing a speech interface and fine-tuning with supervised learning and online distillation techniques. It achieves high scores on benchmarks such as Big Bench Audio (98.90), Speech-BFCL (81.13), and a 65.51% task success rate on τ-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds, demonstrating its capability in speech-conditioned dialogues and reasoning tasks.

item.title: Researchers introduce Safin-1.5, a safety-native architecture with recursive safety improvement and formal reasoning capabilities for large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present Safin-1.5, a model designed to enhance safety alongside general capabilities through recursive self-improvement, combining persistent safety states, hazardous-knowledge disentanglement, and a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The model also integrates a formal reasoning harness that enables symbolic inference and verification during inference time, improving safety and reasoning performance compared to leading models. Safin-1.5's safety architecture retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge while isolating hazardous knowledge into removable components to minimize impact on general capabilities. Its recursive safety improvement process identifies vulnerabilities and develops repair strategies, accepting updates only if they improve safety without excessive refusal. The formal reasoning harness uses proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging to recover missing relations in formal representations, allowing symbolic solvers to construct verifiable proofs under formalized premises. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 outperforms frontier models in both safety and reasoning tasks, indicating its potential for safer and more reliable large language model development through integrated safety mechanisms and verifiable reasoning.

item.title: Researchers introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer reallocating per-block budgets via cross-block equal risk contribution, improving GPT-style model training efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present FARO, a new optimizer for training large language models that adaptively partitions parameters into blocks and reallocates update budgets using a risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. FARO matches the performance of the best hand-designed optimization recipes without manual tuning and achieves modest but consistent improvements in loss reduction across multiple training runs. The approach trims the riskiest parameter blocks rather than expanding the safest, maintaining gains even under corrupted data streams, and the source code is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers evaluate incongruence-aware speech emotion recognition in audio-capable large language models across multiple speech corpora [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score to measure disagreement between text and audio emotion signals in voice-interactive large language models and validated it against human judgment. They evaluated three audio-capable models on acted, conversational, and spontaneous speech datasets, finding that incongruence increases error rates when audio is present, independent of ground-truth emotion and feature space distance. The study suggests that the challenge lies in how models combine raw evidence rather than the signals themselves, with text-only effects proving unreliable. The incongruence score, including a version without an emotion lexicon, consistently predicted errors across all corpora, outperforming simpler alternatives. Code, data tables, and prompts have been released to support further research.

item.title: Researchers introduce Agentic World Modeling to enable parallel test-time scaling of language model agents without environment replication, improving simulation accuracy in shared, non-resettable environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Agentic World Modeling (AWM), a method that allows large language model agents to perform test-time scaling by adaptively querying a shared environment through safe read-only interfaces instead of replicating it. This approach reformulates next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task, enabling parallel exploration without mutating shared state. Evaluations on benchmarks including τ-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench show that AWM outperforms single-shot simulation baselines by over 40% and trained world-model baselines by over 12%, demonstrating its effectiveness for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in realistic enterprise and cloud settings where environment replication is costly or infeasible.

item.title: Researchers present Nedimo, a multilingual AI pipeline generating low-arousal sleep stories with evidence-based engineering and quality controls for relaxation support [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Nedimo, a multilingual AI pipeline designed to generate and narrate low-arousal sleep stories aimed at supporting relaxation and attentional focus rather than clinical sleep treatment. The system incorporates conservative engineering requirements derived from mixed evidence on narrated bedtime audio's effectiveness and includes deterministic planning, large language model generation, and rigorous quality controls such as loudness normalization and error-aware retries. The prototype separates content planning from generation, enforces structural and lexical constraints, and uses a product data model to track user interactions like stop position and replay as behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes. While no clinical efficacy is claimed, the researchers provide an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a guardrail architecture with acceptance thresholds, and a protocol for future testing of sleep-onset effects, positioning Nedimo as a tool whose benefits and potential reliance require empirical evaluation.

item.title: Researchers analyze how large language models anticipate affective responses to gambling and stock outcomes, revealing gain amplification and context-dependent valuation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how large language models (LLMs) predict feelings about gambling and stock-trading outcomes and whether these affective predictions influence their choices. They found that when outcomes were rated individually, LLMs showed diminishing sensitivity to magnitude similar to human value functions but rated gains more intensely than losses, a reversal of typical loss aversion termed silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, ratings became more linear, and the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared in choice behavior, with affective ratings not explaining choices better than monetary utility. These findings indicate that LLMs have flexible mappings from outcomes to affect that differ depending on context and raise questions about how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decision-making processes. The study highlights differences between human and model affective valuation and suggests further exploration is needed on the role of affect in AI decision workflows.

item.title: Researchers propose MOSAIC architecture to separate modality-specific gradients in multi-task learning, improving performance and reducing parameters on Japanese conversation tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce MOSAIC (MOdality-Separated Architecture with Inter-modal Cross-attention), a multi-task learning model that preserves unimodal representations and routes gradients via modality-specific losses to address disproportionate task-modality dependencies. This approach contrasts with conventional fusion-based architectures that enforce unified representations and can dilute task-specific modality importance. On the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation (CEJC), MOSAIC improved average macro-F1 scores by 7.4 points across four tasks while reducing backbone parameters by 72% compared to a fusion-based baseline. The results demonstrate that explicit modality partitioning can yield consistent performance gains with fewer parameters in multi-task, multimodal settings.

item.title: Researchers present Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning to improve LLM agent tool use with deterministic planning and verification, outperforming standard agents by up to 28.9 points [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning (CGAP), a method that enables large language model (LLM) agents to handle natural-language requests by reasoning about required capabilities and available tools. CGAP compiles a tool catalog into a planning model, translates requests into goals using an LLM, and solves the model with a classical planner, ensuring executable plans rather than trial-and-error calls. The approach uses an abstract model tracking input availability without knowing exact outputs, with an LLM adding specific calls during execution and deterministic checks to maintain plan integrity. Each argument is sourced from prior conversation or tool responses, and results are verified by an LLM against the original request. Testing CGAP with three LLMs on multiple benchmarks showed performance improvements of up to 28.9 points over standard tool-calling agents.

item.title: Researchers find greedy parent inheritance drives most optimization gains in LLM-guided prompt and program synthesis, outperforming seed-reset methods across 1,750 runs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated iterative language-model optimizers that refine prompts and programs by showing a proposer model samples of failing cases and keeping improved revisions. They separated the effects of parent inheritance from feedback disclosure across nine benchmarks and 1,750 runs, finding that greedy parent inheritance accounts for the majority of optimization progress and outperforms seed-reset resampling even when the latter uses clustered failure summaries or larger proposer models. While error clustering and diverse failure selection improve early search rounds, sequential parent inheritance quickly closes the gap by retaining solved error modes and filtering failures. The study also analyzed token expenditure in the optimization process, revealing that proposer reflection consumes only a small fraction of the total computational cost, whereas validation and minibatch gating use most of the budget. This suggests that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the benefits of more complex reflective loops with significantly less compute.

item.title: Researchers present RAGFlow, an open-source pipeline that compiles knowledge into structured context for agentic retrieval systems, reducing query tokens and latency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce RAGFlow, a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline that uses a search harness to write, read, and reformulate queries, achieving high accuracy without compiled or vector indexes. The system addresses context inefficiencies by compiling knowledge into structured navigation hierarchies, such as claim-evidence pairs, entity graphs, and timelines, to supply the smallest sufficient context to language models instead of redundant passages. The study finds that while structural artifacts do not improve accuracy under competent harnesses, they significantly reduce query token usage and latency, cutting average tokens by 38% and latency from 140 to 30 seconds. Additional artifacts like ontologies and wikis enhance deployment aspects such as governance and integration. RAGFlow transforms the retrieval loop into five disciplined stages, effectively creating an agent-native database that provides compiled, governed context rather than ranked passage lists.

item.title: TRIDENT and SHAKTI: A Framework and Benchmark for Hindi AI-Text Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.

item.title: SciGraphSelect: Auditable Scientific Data Selection through Knowledge--Reasoning Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific data selection is typically driven by relevance or utility scores, providing limited insight into why a document is retained. We introduce SciGraphSelect, a reference-grounded framework for auditable scientific data selection. SciGraphSelect organizes domain-specific knowledge, reusable reasoning operations, and reference-attested relations into a typed knowledge--reasoning graph, then scores candidate documents using concept coverage, relation and path co-support, and directional alignment. To avoid over-interpreting document embeddings, rich relational structure is preserved on the reference side while candidate-side evidence is treated conservatively without assuming relation entailment. By exposing the reference-grounded evidence behind each selection, SciGraphSelect brings traceability to the upstream construction of scientific training corpora and complements downstream scientific verification.

item.title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution. We introduce SERIAL-7, a Korean-English benchmark built around an executable verification framework for machine-verifiable generation across seven representations. Using 177 validated canonical artifacts, SERIAL-7 separates semantic derivation (Derive), constrained artifact generation (Realize), and cross-representation preservation (Preserve). Its 43 atomic representation constraints are paired with executable checks over format, structure, and task-specific semantics, enabling progressively stricter verification from representation compliance to full artifact validity. Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%, while Full Compliance exposes additional artifact-level failures beyond correct final answers and valid representations. These results show that reliable structured generation requires explicit, executable verification of how artifacts are realized and preserved across representations.

item.title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.

item.title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41396v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.

item.title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41437v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. We designed a large language model (LLM)-based visit preparation agent to guide patients before an appointment by gathering clinical context, setting visit expectations, providing relevant health information, building a prioritized list of questions for their clinician, and generating a summary. In a prospective consented randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults held 866 health-related conversations with the visit preparation agent (standard or concise variant) or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. The visit preparation agent significantly outperformed the control across blinded clinician evaluations and patient self-reports. In clinician reviews of completed sessions (n = 272), the agent achieved a 16.6% higher rate of comprehensive preparation (67.2% vs. 50.6%; P < 0.05) and an 8.5% higher rate of alignment with patients' health context (98.9% vs. 90.4%; P < 0.01), while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness across all study arms. Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed 16.8% higher visit preparedness (73.8% vs. 57.0%; P < 0.01), 14.3% higher confidence in knowing what to ask (81.4% vs. 67.1%; P < 0.01), and 12.0% higher overall satisfaction (74.0% vs. 62.0%; P < 0.05). Clinician and participant metrics were not significantly correlated, indicating that expert review and patient self-assessment capture complementary dimensions of patient-facing AI. These findings suggest that LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and motivate future studies on in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.

item.title: Enhancing Sentiment Classification on Small Datasets through Data Augmentation and Transfer Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small-scale sentiment classification often suffers from data scarcity, which limits the generalization ability of the models. This study evaluates and compares the effectiveness of three data augmentation strategies: Easy Data Augmentation (EDA), back-translation, and contextual token substitution (nlpaug-style), with both traditional machine learning classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest) and transformer-based models (BERT). We perform a comprehensive empirical comparison with low-resource sentiment datasets by summarizing the results of recent studies and performing targeted head-to-head experiments. Our findings indicate that all augmentation methods improve performance. Contextual augmentation yields the most consistent gains for BERT models, while EDA and back-translation provide greater benefits for traditional classifiers. These insights help guide the selection of data augmentation techniques tailored to model type and dataset size, filling a critical gap in research on data augmentation for sentiment classification on small datasets.

item.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41536v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer), and maintains this lead on two out-of-distribution benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that DAPS premises improve theorem proving on miniF2F and IMO-ProofBench. Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.

item.title: GRIT: Gradient Masking for Visually Misgrounded Tokens in Text-Rich Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41629v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

item.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.

item.title: UpLoop: Training Looped Transformers via Upcycling at No Extra Pretraining Compute [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

item.title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at https://github.com/ali-bana/OLMo-Twin.

item.title: Leakage-Controlled Structure-Preserving Augmentation and Template-Aware Evaluation for Bangla Symptom-Based Disease Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bangla symptom-based disease prediction is commonly evaluated on a small, imbalanced structured benchmark containing many profiles that differ by only one or two symptoms. We test whether train-only asymmetric Bernoulli perturbation improves classification using 725 unique profiles spanning 85 diseases and 172 binary symptoms. Experiments use ten repeated real-profile holdouts and parent-grouped inner cross-validation. The 2 x 2 design separates augmentation from hyperparameter tuning, with exact duplication, random oversampling, class weighting, and SMOTEN as balancing controls. For Bernoulli Naive Bayes (BNB), the gain over tuned raw training does not withstand Holm correction, although BNB attains the highest mean accuracy (97.50%). The boosted-tree models benefit substantially: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost improve by 18.10, 28.45, and 10.09 percentage points, respectively. A Hamming-distance audit places 91.0% of standard held-out profiles within one symptom bit of the training data. Accuracy decreases on a same-disease 1-bit-purged challenge; nevertheless, XGBoost and LightGBM retain large augmentation gains. We also evaluate robustness to missing and spurious symptoms and the faithfulness of BNB explanations. Overall, Bernoulli perturbation is useful for some model families, but benchmark accuracy should be interpreted together with template proximity.

item.title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.

item.title: DAMI: Dual-Axis Memory Initialization for Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval in Gated Linear Attention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.41994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.

item.title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.42000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.

item.title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.42066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.

item.title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.42149v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity.
